rationale: Start with a broad mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to spread unknown compounds across the run while keeping most species likely to elute within 42 min. This should reveal overall retention range, crowding zones, and whether stronger/weaker or steeper/shallower gradients are needed next.

All 10 compounds eluted early with excellent resolution, so the limitation is analysis time rather than separation. Doubling the gradient time while keeping composition and temperature fixed should test whether a shallower gradient can preserve full resolution and shift the last peak later toward a more time-optimal CRF region.

The first run already had perfect resolution, so we should shorten total retention while preserving the broad separation window. A slightly stronger overall gradient span with a shorter gradient should pull the last peak later enough to remain informative but reduce the time penalty versus the 20 min method.

Injection 3 is very close to ideal, so the next move is a small local refinement to further reduce the time term while checking that the tightest cluster around peaks 5–7 remains above the resolution threshold. A slightly steeper gradient is the most direct way to probe whether CRF can be nudged even closer to 1.0.

We are in a near-optimal region, but the limiting factor is the 6/7 pair at R = 1.20. Lowering temperature slightly while keeping the successful fast gradient fixed may improve selectivity enough to lift that pair above threshold without sacrificing much run time.

The best region is still the 14 min high-span gradient, with the central cluster limiting CRF. Since lowering temperature hurt selectivity, the complementary local probe is to raise temperature slightly and see whether the 6/7 pair separates better while keeping the zero time penalty.

Temperature changes worsened the critical cluster, so keep 40 C and probe selectivity through gradient shape instead. Raising phi0 slightly should compress the earliest, over-resolved peaks and may redistribute the crowded mid-eluters enough to improve the worst-pair resolution while preserving the zero time penalty region.

Increasing phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved CRF, so one more step in the same direction is the best local search move. This should further compress the noncritical early region and may slightly reshape the crowded middle pair while staying in the no-time-penalty regime.

The best method so far is 0.10/0.95, 14 min, 40 C, but the 6/7 pair is still limiting. A small increase in tG at the improved phi0 should be the most likely way to raise that critical resolution above the current best while remaining near the optimum time window.

We are extremely close to the maximum, so only a fine local probe is justified. Since phi0 = 0.10 outperformed 0.05 and 0.15 at tG = 14, testing phi0 = 0.15 at tG = 16 checks whether the slightly longer gradient shifts the optimum phi0 upward and can remove the tiny remaining time penalty without losing full resolution.

CRF is already at the maximum, so any further run is purely confirmatory/local mapping around the optimum. Increasing phi0 one step tests the edge of the plateau and whether an even faster-retaining profile still preserves full resolution and maximum CRF.

The optimum is clearly local around phi0 = 0.15, tG = 16, 40 C, so the remaining useful check is whether a slightly weaker phi1 keeps all compounds eluting with full resolution while maintaining the maximum score. This maps the other side of the gradient-strength plateau around the current optimum.

The current optimum is confirmed, and lowering phi1 slightly to 0.90 kept full resolution with only a tiny time penalty. One more step down in phi1 usefully defines the robustness boundary on the weaker-gradient side and tests whether the score plateau extends there.

With a maximum CRF already achieved, the only worthwhile follow-up is to map how broad the optimum is around the critical 6/7 pair. Extending tG one step from the near-optimal 0.10/0.95/16/40 condition tests whether extra selectivity margin can be gained while still potentially remaining on the score plateau.

The optimum is already found, so this is just to map the local neighborhood around the best method. Testing the best phi0 with a slightly longer gradient checks whether the extra selectivity margin remains compatible with the maximum-score plateau or incurs a time penalty similar to the phi0 = 0.10 case.

A maximum-score method is already identified, so this run is only to assess robustness of the optimum to temperature. Checking +5 C at the best composition/gradient maps whether the method is sharply temperature-dependent or remains near-optimal under a modest thermal shift.

The best method is already known, so the only remaining value is robustness mapping; +5 C strongly degraded the critical pair, suggesting a sharp temperature dependence. Running the symmetric -5 C test at the optimum composition/gradient will define the temperature window around the maximum and whether 40 C is truly the selectivity optimum.

The optimum has been found and temperature robustness mapped, so a final useful local check is whether a longer gradient at the exact best composition gains substantial resolution margin before time penalty becomes excessive. This defines the selectivity-versus-time tradeoff boundary around the optimum method.

With the optimum already achieved, the only remaining informative direction is the faster side of the local optimum. Shortening tG one step from the best method tests how sharply CRF falls on the steep-gradient side and brackets the score maximum around tG = 16 min.

The optimum is established, so a remaining useful experiment is to see whether reducing both ends of the gradient from the best neighborhood preserves the score plateau. This tests whether the method is robust to a narrower, slightly weaker gradient window while keeping the same temperature and gradient time.

A distinct nearby condition can still map the extent of the optimum plateau on the faster and slightly weaker-gradient side. This tests whether the best method remains near-maximal when both gradient duration and final strength are reduced together.

A maximum has already been reached, so the remaining value is mapping the nearby plateau edges in composition space. Combining the higher phi0 that was still strong with the weaker phi1 that remained fully resolved tests another untried flank around the optimum.

A second maximum-score point has now been found, so the best remaining use of injections is to define the faster edge of this newly identified optimum plateau. Shortening tG by one step tests whether this composition pair can keep CRF at 1.000 with an even steeper gradient or if the critical pair immediately drops below the threshold.

Two maximum-score methods define a plateau, and the next informative step is to test whether that plateau extends to even higher phi0 at the same tG and phi1. This probes the upper edge of the composition window while staying in the successful 16 min, 40 C region.

The plateau includes 0.20/0.90/16/40, while pushing phi0 to 0.25 caused early coelution, so the last informative edge test is to lower phi1 one step at phi0 = 0.20. This probes whether the second maximum extends toward a weaker final strength without sacrificing the critical separations.
